lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Classify: wooden block; juice; helium in a balloon; honey.

FEEDBACK
Solid; liquid; gas; liquid (thick).

WATCH FOR
Thinking gases aren’t real materials because we can’t see them misses air evidence (wind, bubbles).
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Sort fifteen everyday materials into solid/liquid/gas with one property reason each. Note one material that changes state when heated/cooled.

Write a short reflection naming one observation or step you corrected and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Solids keep their shape; liquids take the shape of a container and can be poured; gases spread to fill available space and are often invisible.
materials: Optional: safe everyday objects for observation
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.
lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Sort fifteen everyday materials into solid/liquid/gas with one property reason each. Note one material that changes state when heated/cooled. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Original response on new material: Solid; liquid; gas; liquid (thick). Reasoning: I used solid by attending to liquid rather than copying the worked model.

Parent: Written model 2: Common error: Thinking gases aren’t real materials because we can’t see them misses air evidence (wind, bubbles). Correction: Solid; liquid; gas; liquid (thick). Why: the correction restores accurate use of solid.

Parent: Likely misconception: Thinking gases aren’t real materials because we can’t see them misses air evidence (wind, bubbles). Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Investigate or describe a fresh example (not the worked objects) that uses solid. Record evidence and explain how it supports your claim.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one science misconception about solid, correct it with evidence, and say why the correction works.

Parent: Marking notes: Require a new example, named observations and a claim–evidence link. / Require misconception + corrected claim + evidence reason..

Solids keep their shape; liquids take the shape of a container and can be poured; gases spread to fill available space and are often invisible.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen or measured.
